REUTERS/Nathan Howard President Donald Trump and his family could soon be confronted with “one of the biggest scandals” he’s ever faced, scholar and journalist Sidney Blumenthal argued in a video published Saturday on the legal commentary network “Legal AF.” At the heart of the potential scandal is the recent arrest of MAGA influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate, both of whom are facing extradition on charges involving human trafficking, rape and child pornography. “We have a scandal that is one of the biggest scandals of the Trump administration and its dimensions are literally unknown right now. And there’s a call for an investigation , we have not gotten to the bottom of it,” Blumenthal said. “If you think it’s just about the Tate brothers, you’re wrong because the Tate brothers’ extradition to the United Kingdom is just the tip of the iceberg of what may be the greatest international crime syndicate with the greatest political influence in history… it’s about the politics and the network at the center of the Trump world where the Trump world is an underworld.” Joining Blumenthal for the discussion was investigative reporter Nina Burleigh , who, as a journalist who had investigated Jeffrey Epstein for years, dubbed the Tate brothers as the “millennial version of Epstein.” The Tate brothers were previously arrested on rape and human trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, but after pressure from the Trump administration, were allowed to leave the country. Since then, Burleigh noted, both brothers have been “welcomed back into the fold” by Trump’s allies. “They were invited to the White House , they were at the Milken conference with Paolo Zampolli , Trump’s special envoy for special projects, and they were swatting all over the world,” Burleigh said. “So basically given a free pass by the United States government to our great shame, and they have lived here for the past year and a half.” Burleigh also flagged another key figure in Trump’s inner circle: Richard Grenell , the president’s envoy for special missions, who she claimed “played a key role in springing the Tates from Romania,” and was “closely tied” to the brothers. “Rick Grenell went over to Romania and pressured the government to allow these guys to leave the country. So right there, you have material for investigation because that was a foreign legal matter that our country went over and put the thumbscrews to spring these two guys,” she said. “They’re the millennial version of Epstein; they have a type of network that is similar in that it relies on the trading of females and the abuse of women as the glue that connects them to each other. But it’s also a financial and political power node that they inhabit.” Trump's Link to Tate Brothers Exposed by Inner Circle! by Legal AF Read on Substack SmartNews Trump News Stories Chosen For You ALSO READ: 'God's money': White House enrages with vow that public cash belongs to evangelicals Should Trump be forced to release his financial records? In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic ‌train carrying former British ​Prime ⁠Minister Boris Johnson and other ⁠European ​diplomats had been at the station. Russia carried out two drone strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border on Sunday Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS What did EU leaders say about the train attack? "It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said. "I ​think we should act the opposite. ​We should show that we are ⁠there ​for Ukraine ​and we are ​not scared," ‌she told reporters in ​Finland, ⁠where she attended ⁠ a ​summit on Arctic strategy. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow. "For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said. "We are united here in Europe," he added. Amid Russia's war Ukraine, Poland reconcile painful past To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us." "We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said. French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them." Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years. "Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said. Germany warns against escalation with Russia German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution. "I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said. The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so. Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe. "Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said. Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: 1:39 CCTV footage shows police shootout after Kraków attack – video Poland Two police officers hailed as heroes for confronting Kraków gunman Jakub Kulik critically injured and Artur Morański also wounded after actions that ‘prevented further casualties’ Angela Giuffrida Sun 8 Nov 2026 16.11 EST First published on Sun 8 Nov 2026 09.49 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Polish police officers who were injured as they pursued and detained the gunman in Kraków on Saturday have been hailed as heroes. One of them is Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, who was left critically injured after a close-range exchange of fire with the suspect, a 24-year-old Polish national who killed six and injured 17 in an attack believed to have been inspired by far-right ideologies. The other injured police officer is Artur Morański. Both are under 30 years old, the Polish news network TVP World reported. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Saturday in a post on X: “They probably saved many human lives, disregarding the risk to their own.” The Polish justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said the rapid response and heroism of the two police officers “prevented further human casualties”. Police arrived at the scene 23 seconds after receiving the first emergency call from Kraków’s main square, where the suspect was shooting at random from his car. Footage that emerged on Sunday showed two police officers exchanging fire with the gunman. One of the officers then apprehended the suspect on the ground before firing his own weapon several times. The officer then fell down, apparently injured himself. Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, stepped in to help. Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help”, Pędziwiatr told the Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.” View image in fullscreen The scene after the shootings in Kraków. Photograph: Reuters Kulik, from the southern Polish city of Bielsko-Biala, was hit by three bullets and underwent surgery on Saturday. There has been a national appeal for blood donors. Morański was shot in the chest area and also underwent surgery. Both men were brought out of medically induced comas on Sunday, Polskie Radio 24 reported. Kulik is also a member of the volunteer fire service in Bielsko-Biala. “We’re very proud of him,” a volunteer firefighter from the city’s Leszczyny district told the local news website Bielsko.biala.pl . “He responds to emergencies just like we do.” TVP World reported that Morański was from Powroźnik, a village about 90 miles (150km) south-east of Krakow and close to the border with Slovakia. A mass was held for him at the local church on Sunday.
